rcon-component-001.explanation: **The concept:** A component is the unit of UI in React: a plain JavaScript function that takes one argument (the props object) and returns JSX. The whole app is a tree of these functions calling each other through markup. **Why it matters:** Components give you the same powers functions give logic — naming, reuse, isolation, testability. Instead of one page of tangled markup you get `<Header />`, `<ProductList />`, `<Footer />`, each understandable alone. **How React uses it:** React calls your function whenever it needs to know what that part of the screen looks like (first render, and again whenever props or state change). Your function should be pure: same props in, same JSX out, no side effects during rendering. **Common mistakes:** Lowercase names (React treats `<profile />` as an unknown HTML tag); defining a component inside another component's body (it becomes a new function every render, so React unmounts and remounts it, losing state); calling a component as a function (`Profile()`) instead of rendering it (`<Profile />`), which breaks hooks and reconciliation.

rcon-jsx-001.explanation:
**The concept:** JSX is syntax sugar over function calls. `

Hi

` compiles (via Vite/Babel/TypeScript) to `jsx('h1', { className: 'big', children: 'Hi' })`, which returns a cheap element object — a description, not a DOM node. **Why it exists:** Rendering logic and markup are inherently coupled (conditions decide what to show, loops produce lists), so React co-locates them in one language instead of splitting logic into a template dialect. **The rules that differ from HTML:** one root element per return (wrap siblings in a fragment `<>…`); every tag closes (``, `
`); attributes are camelCase JS identifiers (`className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`); curly braces embed any expression — but statements like `if` and `for` don't fit, so you use ternaries, `&&`, and `.map()`. **Common mistakes:** Forgetting that `{}` takes expressions only; using `class` instead of `className`; rendering `0` accidentally via `count && ` (use `count > 0 && …`); expecting JSX to be sanitizing HTML input — it escapes embedded strings, which is different from parsing HTML.

resources.label: react.dev — JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces

rcon-state-001.explanation: **The concept:** State is data a component remembers between renders and that drives what it shows. `useState(initial)` returns the current value and a setter; calling the setter stores the new value and asks React to re-render. **Why a setter, not assignment:** A component is just a function — local variables die when it returns, and React has no way to notice a mutation. The setter is the signal: "my data changed, render me again." On the next call React hands back the stored value. **Key behaviors:** State updates are batched and applied before the next render, so reading the state variable right after calling the setter still gives the old value (it's a snapshot of this render). When the next value depends on the previous, pass a function: `setCount(c => c + 1)` — three of these in a row add 3, while `setCount(count + 1)` three times adds 1. Objects and arrays must be replaced, not mutated: `setUser({ ...user, name })`. **Common mistakes:** Mutating state in place (React sees the same reference and may skip the render); mirroring props into state "to edit them" when derived values should just be computed during render; storing values that never affect the UI in state instead of a `useRef`.

rcon-lifecycle-001.explanation: **The concept:** Every component mounts (first appears), updates (re-renders with new props/state), and unmounts (is removed). Class components exposed these as methods; function components express them through `useEffect`, which synchronizes the component with things outside React (timers, subscriptions, network, the DOM). **How the pieces map:** effect with `[]` deps → runs once after mount (componentDidMount); effect with `[a, b]` → runs after mount and after any render where `a` or `b` changed (componentDidUpdate, but scoped); the returned cleanup function → runs before every re-run and at unmount (componentWillUnmount). **The mental model shift:** Don't think "lifecycle events", think synchronization: the effect says "keep this external thing consistent with these values", and cleanup undoes the previous sync before the next one. **Common mistakes:** Missing dependencies (the effect closes over stale values — the classic stale closure bug); forgetting cleanup, leaking intervals and listeners; using effects for derived state that should just be computed during render; putting data transformations in effects when they belong in event handlers or render.

rcon-hooks-001.explanation: **The concept:** Hooks are React's API for giving function components capabilities that used to require classes: state, lifecycle, context, refs. Each is a `use*` function called during render. The core set: `useState` (memory), `useEffect` (external synchronization), `useContext` (read context), `useRef` (mutable box / DOM handle that doesn't trigger renders), `useMemo`/`useCallback` (cache values/functions between renders), `useReducer` (state with reducer logic). **Why the rules exist:** React stores hook data in a list attached to the component instance and matches each `use*` call to its slot **by call order**. That's why hooks must run unconditionally at the top level — an `if` around a hook shifts every later hook one slot over, corrupting all of them. The `react-hooks` ESLint plugin enforces this. **The superpower:** Because hooks are plain functions, you can compose them into custom hooks (`useForm`, `useFetch`) — stateful logic becomes as reusable as any utility function, with no wrapper components. **Common mistakes:** Calling hooks inside conditions/loops/callbacks; calling them from regular functions (only components and other hooks may); over-reaching for `useEffect` when an event handler is the right home for the logic.

rcon-composition-001.explanation: **The concept:** Composition means building bigger components out of smaller ones the way you build expressions out of functions — nesting, not inheriting. Data flows down through props; whole pieces of UI flow down through the special `children` prop (whatever you put between a component's tags) or any prop that holds JSX. **The patterns:** `children` for generic containers (`Card`, `Modal`, `Layout` don't need to know what they wrap); multiple "slot" props (`header={<Logo />} sidebar={<Nav />}`) when a component has several holes to fill; lifting state up when siblings need to share data — the state moves to their common parent, which passes it down. **Why not inheritance:** Extending a base component couples you to its internals and creates rigid hierarchies. Props and children solve every customization case — React's own docs say they've found no use case where inheritance is preferable. **Common mistakes:** Prop drilling five levels because state was lifted higher than needed (or context was avoided when appropriate); cloning and patching children instead of designing explicit props; giant "god components" that render everything instead of delegating.

resources.label: react.dev — Passing Props to a Component

rcon-reactdom-001.explanation: **The concept:** React is split in two packages. `react` defines components, elements, state, hooks — it knows nothing about browsers. `react-dom` is the renderer that turns that element tree into real DOM nodes and keeps them updated. **The API surface you use:** `createRoot(domNode).render(<App />)` bootstraps a client app; `hydrateRoot` attaches to server-rendered HTML; `createPortal(children, otherDomNode)` renders part of the tree into a different DOM location (modals, tooltips) while keeping it in the same React tree for context and events; `react-dom/server` renders to HTML strings/streams. **Why the split matters:** The reconciler is renderer-agnostic, which is how React Native (native views), react-three-fiber (WebGL), and ink (terminals) exist — same components and hooks, different output. It also explains why you install two packages and why `renderToString` lives under `react-dom/server`, not `react`. **Common mistakes:** Calling `createRoot` more than once on the same node instead of calling `root.render` again; manually mutating DOM that React owns (React will overwrite it on the next render); forgetting portals still bubble events through the React tree, not the DOM tree.

rcon-vdom-001.explanation: **The concept:** When a component renders, it doesn't touch the DOM — it returns a tree of plain objects (React elements) describing the desired UI. React keeps the tree from the previous render, diffs the new one against it ("reconciliation"), and applies only the differences to the real DOM. Creating objects is cheap; DOM mutation and the layout/paint it triggers are expensive — so React spends cheap CPU to minimize expensive DOM work. **How the diff works:** It's O(n) because of two heuristics. Same element type at the same position → keep the DOM node, patch changed attributes, recurse into children. Different type (`<div>` → `<span>`, or `ComponentA` → `ComponentB`) → tear the subtree down and rebuild it, destroying its state. For lists, React matches children across renders by `key`, so reorders move DOM nodes instead of rewriting their contents. **Why keys must be stable:** With `key={index}`, inserting an item at the top shifts every index — React thinks every row changed and, worse, row state (like an input's text) sticks to the position, not the item. A stable id makes the diff match items correctly. **Common mistakes:** Index keys on reorderable lists; assuming the virtual DOM makes everything fast (it reduces DOM writes, not your render cost — a slow render is still slow); thinking a re-render always means DOM changes (usually the diff finds nothing to do).

rcon-forms-001.explanation: **The concept:** HTML inputs keep their own value in the DOM; React state lives in components. Forms force you to pick who owns the value. Controlled: React owns it — `value={state}` + `onChange` writing back to state; the input shows exactly what state says, always. Uncontrolled: the DOM owns it — you set `defaultValue` and read the value when you need it (via a ref, or `new FormData(form)` on submit). **When each fits:** Controlled shines when the UI reacts as the user types — live validation, character counters, formatting, enabling/disabling submit, filtering a list. Uncontrolled is less code when you only care about the final value at submit time. **Submission:** In an SPA you handle `onSubmit` on the `<form>`, call `e.preventDefault()` to stop the browser's page-reloading POST, and use the values from state (controlled) or FormData (uncontrolled). **Common mistakes:** `value` without `onChange` — React locks the field to the state value and the user can't type (use `defaultValue` if you wanted uncontrolled); switching an input between controlled and uncontrolled by letting state become `undefined`; storing each keystroke of a big form in a parent that re-renders an expensive tree.

resources.label: react.dev — Reacting to Input with State

rcon-context-001.explanation: **The problem it solves:** Some data is needed by many components at different depths — theme, locale, the signed-in user. Passing it as props through every intermediate component ("prop drilling") couples layers that don't care about the data. **How it works:** `createContext(defaultValue)` creates a channel. A `<Ctx.Provider value={…}>` publishes a value for its subtree; any descendant calls `useContext(Ctx)` and gets the **nearest** provider's value above it. No provider → the default. Providers nest: an inner provider shadows an outer one for its subtree. **The performance rule:** When a provider's `value` changes (by `Object.is`), every component that reads that context re-renders. Two consequences: don't create the value object inline on every parent render (`value={{ user, setUser }}` makes a new object each time — memoize it), and split fast-changing state out of contexts holding slow-changing data. **Common mistakes:** Using context for everything ("a global store") when most state belongs near where it's used; forgetting that only components calling `useContext` subscribe — intermediate components don't re-render just for being in between; not wrapping the provider high enough, so a consumer silently gets the default value.

react.dev — Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

rcon-performance-001.explanation: **The baseline:** When a component re-renders, all its children re-render by default — usually fine, because rendering is cheap and the virtual DOM diff discards no-op changes. Optimize only what the React DevTools Profiler shows is actually slow. **The memoization trio:** `memo(Component)` skips re-rendering a child when its props are shallow-equal to last time. But props compared by reference break it: a parent that creates `() => …` or `{…}` inline passes a new reference every render. That's what the other two fix — `useCallback(fn, deps)` keeps the same function reference across renders, `useMemo(() => value, deps)` keeps the same computed value/object reference (and also caches genuinely expensive computations). The three work as a system; `memo` alone rarely survives real props. **Beyond memoization:** stable `key`s so list diffs match items; `React.lazy` + `Suspense` to code-split rarely-used routes out of the initial bundle; virtualization (react-window) for lists with thousands of rows; moving state down so typing in an input doesn't re-render the whole page. **Common mistakes:** Wrapping everything in `useCallback`/`useMemo` "for speed" (each adds its own bookkeeping cost and complexity); measuring in dev mode (dev builds are much slower than production); missing that a context value or a `children` element created inline defeats `memo` just like any other prop.

rcon-reuse-001.explanation: **The problem:** Several components need the same stateful behavior — subscribe to window size, fetch and cache data, track a form field. Copy-pasting the `useState` + `useEffect` plumbing into each one duplicates bugs. **Custom hooks (the modern answer):** Extract the logic into a function named `use*` that calls other hooks and returns whatever the component needs. Each component calling it gets its **own independent state** — hooks share logic, not state. This composes cleanly (a custom hook can use other custom hooks) and adds zero components to the tree. **The legacy patterns you'll still meet:** Higher-order components — `withAuth(Component)` returns a wrapped component with extra props injected; used by older Redux (`connect`) and React Router (`withRouter`). Render props — `<DataSource render={(data) => <List items={data} />} />`, the child receives values through a function prop. Both work but nest: three HOCs deep and DevTools shows a pyramid of wrappers, and where a prop came from becomes a mystery. Hooks flattened all of it. **Common mistakes:** Naming a helper `useX` when it calls no hooks (or calling hooks in a non-`use` function, breaking lint rules); returning too much from a hook instead of a focused API; reaching for an HOC in new code where a hook is simpler.

resources.label: react.dev — Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

rcon-security-001.explanation: **The main threat — XSS:** Cross-site scripting means attacker-controlled text ends up executing as code in your users' browsers. React's default is safe: any value embedded as `{text}` is escaped before insertion — `<script>` becomes harmless text. Attacks therefore target the escape hatches. **The escape hatches to audit:** `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` inserts raw HTML — only ever feed it sanitized output (DOMPurify is the standard); URLs in `href`/`src` — `javascript:alert(1)` executes on click, so validate protocol (`http:`/`https:`) for user-supplied links; spreading untrusted objects (`{...userData}`) into elements can smuggle in dangerous props; server-rendered JSON injected into HTML templates needs escaping too. **Beyond XSS:** Everything in the bundle is public — API keys, "hidden" admin routes, environment variables baked in at build time (`VITE_*`) are all readable by anyone; client-side route guards and disabled buttons are UX, not access control — every check must exist on the server too; keep dependencies patched (`npm audit`) since the supply chain is part of your attack surface. **Common mistakes:** Sanitizing on the client but not on the server (or vice versa — do it where the HTML is produced for rendering); trusting data from your own API that originally came from users; putting a secret in `VITE_SOMETHING` and assuming it's hidden.

resources.label: OWASP — Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

rcon-typecheck-001.explanation: **The concept:** Typechecking catches "wrong prop, wrong shape" bugs before users do. Two generations of tools: PropTypes (runtime, legacy) and TypeScript (compile time, the modern standard). **TypeScript in practice:** Declare a type for the props object and annotate the destructured parameter. The compiler then checks every call site: missing required props, wrong types, typos in prop names — all red squiggles before the code runs. It also types your state (`useState<Item[]>([])`), event handlers (`ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`), refs, and context, which PropTypes never covered. Union types shine for UI: `variant: 'primary' | 'danger'` makes invalid variants unrepresentable. **PropTypes:** A separate `prop-types` package; you attach `Component.propTypes = { name: PropTypes.string.isRequired }` and get console warnings at runtime in development only. You'll see it in older codebases and interview questions, but it verifies nothing at build time and nothing in production. **Common mistakes:** Typing props as `any` (opts out of the whole point); overusing `React.FC` (works, but the plain annotated-parameter style is what react.dev and this repo use); forgetting `children: ReactNode` when a component wraps content.

rcon-redux-001.explanation: **The concept:** Redux moves shared app state out of the component tree into one store — a single state object updated by a strict protocol. Components can't change state directly; they **dispatch actions** (plain objects like `{ type: 'cart/itemAdded', payload }`), and **reducers** — pure functions `(state, action) => newState` — compute the next state. The store notifies subscribers, the UI re-reads. **Why the ceremony:** Every change is an explicit, serializable action, so state becomes predictable and debuggable — Redux DevTools shows a timeline of every action and the state after each, with time-travel. Reducers being pure makes updates testable with no mocks. **Redux Toolkit is the way you actually write it:** `createSlice` generates action types and creators from your reducer names, and uses Immer so you write `state.value += 1` while immutability is preserved under the hood. `configureStore` wires slices together and sets up DevTools + sensible middleware by default. Hand-rolled `createStore` + switch-statement reducers is the legacy style RTK replaced. **When to use it:** Substantial shared state, updated from many places, where you want the audit trail. For "just avoid prop drilling", context is enough; for "cache server data", RTK Query or React Query fit better. **Common mistakes:** Putting local UI state (an open dropdown) in the store; mutating state in a non-Immer reducer; doing async work or side effects inside reducers (they must stay pure).

resources.label: redux.js.org — Redux Essentials: Overview and Concepts

rcon-reactredux-001.explanation: **The concept:** Redux itself is framework-agnostic — `store.getState()`, `store.dispatch()`, `store.subscribe()`. React Redux is the official binding that turns those into idiomatic React: `<Provider store={store}>` puts the store in context, `useSelector` reads a slice of state and subscribes the component to it, `useDispatch` returns the dispatch function for firing actions. **How useSelector decides to re-render:** After every dispatched action it re-runs your selector and compares the result to the previous one **by reference** (`===`). Different → the component re-renders; same → nothing happens. Two consequences: select the narrowest value you need (`state.cart.total`, not `state`), and never return a fresh object/array from a selector (`state.items.filter(…)` creates a new array every time → re-render on every action; memoize with `createSelector` from Reselect instead). **Typed usage:** Derive `RootState` and `AppDispatch` from the store and use them in your selectors and dispatch — the standard TS pattern from the Redux docs (often wrapped once as `useAppSelector`/`useAppDispatch`). **Common mistakes:** Forgetting the Provider (hooks throw "could not find react-redux context"); selecting the whole state object; dispatching in render instead of in handlers/effects; the legacy `connect(mapStateToProps)` HOC still appears in older code — hooks replaced it.

rcon-reduxasync-001.explanation: **The problem:** Reducers must be pure — no fetch, no timers, no randomness — because Redux may replay them (DevTools time-travel) and purity is what makes state predictable. But real apps fetch data. Async work therefore lives in **middleware**, the layer between `dispatch` and the reducers. **Thunks — the standard:** With the thunk middleware (included by `configureStore`), you can dispatch a function instead of an action. `createAsyncThunk` packages the whole pattern: give it an action type prefix and an async function; it returns a thunk that automatically dispatches `pending` when it starts, `fulfilled` with the resolved value, or `rejected` with the error. Your slice handles those three in `extraReducers` to drive the canonical `status`/`data`/`error` shape — the loading spinner, the happy path, and the error message all become plain synchronous state updates. **The flow end to end:** component dispatches `fetchUser(id)` → middleware runs the async function → lifecycle actions hit the reducers → store updates → `useSelector` re-renders the component at each step. **The alternatives:** RTK Query (part of Redux Toolkit) generates hooks like `useGetUserQuery(id)` with caching, deduplication, and invalidation — preferred for pure server-data fetching; redux-saga handles complex long-running flows (debounce, cancellation, sequences) with generators, common in older large apps. **Common mistakes:** Fetching inside a reducer; not handling `rejected` (errors vanish silently); duplicating server data into hand-written thunks when RTK Query would manage it for you.

resources.label: redux.js.org — Redux Essentials: Async Logic and Data Fetching

rcon-routing-001.explanation: **The concept:** In a classic website every navigation asks the server for a new HTML page. In an SPA the app loads once; "navigation" means updating the URL with the History API and swapping which components render — instant, state-preserving, no reload. The router is the library that keeps URL ⇄ UI in sync. **React Router's pieces:** `<BrowserRouter>` connects to the browser history; `<Routes>`/`<Route path element>` declare the URL-to-component mapping, including dynamic segments (`/users/:id`) and a `*` catch-all for 404s; `<Link to>`/`<NavLink>` navigate without reloading (never use `<a href>` internally — it reloads the app and drops all state); `useParams()` reads the dynamic segments, `useNavigate()` navigates imperatively (e.g. after a form submit), `useSearchParams()` reads/writes the query string. Nested routes render child routes into a parent's `<Outlet />` — how this app's `/:subject/*` screens share `SubjectLayout`. **The URL is state:** Put shareable state (filters, search, active tab) in the URL, not just component state — this repo's card library does exactly that with `useSearchParams`. **The deployment gotcha:** The server never hears about client-side navigations, but a hard refresh on `/users/42` does hit the server — it must serve `index.html` for every path (this repo's `vercel.json` rewrite), or deep links 404. **Common mistakes:** `<a>` instead of `<Link>`; forgetting the catch-all route; keeping filter state in `useState` where it can't be bookmarked.

rcon-testing-001.explanation: **The stack:** A runner executes tests in a simulated browser environment — Jest with jsdom (this repo) or Vitest in newer Vite projects. React Testing Library (RTL) renders your component into that DOM and gives you queries; `@testing-library/user-event` simulates clicks and typing the way a browser fires them; `@testing-library/jest-dom` adds readable matchers (`toBeInTheDocument`, `toBeDisabled`). **The philosophy:** "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you." Query by what users perceive — role and accessible name (`getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`), label, visible text — never by class names, ids, or component internals. Tests written this way survive refactors: rewrite the component's internals completely and the test still passes as long as the behavior holds. Bonus: if `getByRole` can't find your button, users of assistive tech can't either. **Async UI:** `findBy*` queries wait for elements that appear after effects or data loading; `await userEvent.click(…)` handles the event → state → re-render cycle. **What to test:** behavior ("clicking Add shows the item"), edge states (empty, loading, error), accessibility of interactive elements — not implementation details like state values or that a specific hook was called. **Common mistakes:** `getByTestId` everywhere (last resort only); asserting on internal state instead of visible output; snapshot-testing whole pages (fails on every change, reviews become rubber stamps); forgetting to await user-event calls.

rcon-building-001.explanation: **Why a build step exists:** Browsers don't understand JSX or TypeScript, and shipping hundreds of separate module files with full comments and whitespace would be slow. The build pipeline: transpile (JSX → `jsx()` calls, TS → JS, modern syntax → target syntax), bundle (merge the module graph into a few files), tree-shake (drop unimported code), minify, and fingerprint (`index-a1b2c3.js` hashed names so browsers cache aggressively but pick up new deploys). **Vite's model:** In dev, no bundling at all — files are transformed on demand and served as native ES modules, so the server starts in milliseconds regardless of app size, and HMR (hot module replacement) swaps edited modules in place, preserving component state. For production, `vite build` runs Rollup to produce the optimized `dist/`. Configuration is one plugin: `@vitejs/plugin-react`. **Code splitting:** Dynamic `import()` becomes a separate chunk loaded on demand — this app's per-subject JSON banks each become their own chunk exactly this way; `React.lazy` does the same for components/routes. **Env vars:** `import.meta.env.VITE_*` values are string-replaced **at build time** — they're public, in the bundle, readable by anyone; a rebuild is needed to change them. **The lineage:** webpack + Babel powered Create React App for years; CRA is deprecated and Vite is the default for client-rendered React today (react.dev now points framework-less users to it). **Common mistakes:** Committing `dist/`; treating `VITE_*` as secrets; testing only in dev mode and missing prod-only issues (run `vite preview`).

rcon-ssr-001.explanation: **The problem with pure client rendering:** The server sends an empty `<div id="root">`, then the browser downloads the bundle, runs React, fetches data — the user stares at a blank page meanwhile, and crawlers that don't run JS see nothing. **What SSR does:** On each request, the server runs your components (`renderToString`, or the streaming `renderToPipeableStream`) and sends real HTML — content is visible immediately. The browser then loads the same component code and calls `hydrateRoot`: instead of building DOM from scratch, React walks the existing server-produced markup, adopts it, and attaches event handlers. After hydration it's a normal SPA. **The hydration contract:** The first client render must produce exactly what the server produced. Anything non-deterministic — `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, locale formatting that differs between server and browser, browser-only branches (`typeof window`) — causes hydration mismatch warnings, and React may throw away the server HTML and re-render. **The trade-offs:** Faster first contentful paint and reliable SEO, but you now run and scale a Node server, components must survive an environment with no `window`, and the page isn't interactive until hydration completes. **Why frameworks:** Wiring SSR by hand means a server, per-route data fetching before render, serializing that data to the client, and code-splitting coordination — Next.js and Remix/React Router handle this, plus streaming and React Server Components in Next's App Router. **Common mistakes:** Touching `window`/`localStorage` during render (crashes on the server — move it into `useEffect`); rendering timestamps that differ across the boundary; assuming SSR is free performance (it trades server compute for client latency).

rcon-ssg-001.explanation: **The concept:** SSG runs the same rendering as SSR but **once, at build time**, for every page — the output is a folder of ready-made HTML files served from a CDN. No server renders anything at request time; every visitor gets the same instantly-delivered file, which then hydrates into an interactive React app exactly like SSR output does. **SSR vs SSG is only "when":** per request (SSR — content can differ per user/visit) versus per deploy (SSG — content identical for everyone until the next build). That's why SSG is the fastest and cheapest option (CDN + no compute) and why it can't do per-user content without client-side fetching on top. **Where it shines / breaks:** Perfect for docs, blogs, marketing sites, product catalogs that change on deploy. Breaks down with thousands of pages (build time grows with page count) or minute-by-minute freshness — Next.js's ISR (incremental static regeneration) patches that by re-rendering individual pages in the background after a revalidate window, giving static speed with bounded staleness. **In Next.js:** Pages without request-time data are statically rendered by default; `generateStaticParams` enumerates the concrete paths to prebuild for dynamic routes like `/posts/[slug]`. Dedicated SSG tools: Astro (islands architecture), Gatsby historically. **Common mistakes:** Choosing SSG for dashboards or logged-in content (it's baked at build time); forgetting to trigger a rebuild/revalidate when the CMS content changes; conflating "static site" with "no JavaScript" — hydrated SSG pages are full React apps.
